issues.legal_issue: A short delay by an eyewitness in naming the assailants after a shocking attack does not, by itself, make the eyewitness’s account unreliable.
material_facts: The witness was accompanying and guarding the deceased when the attack occurred and saw it.
When the witness first reached the deceased’s home, he did not immediately name the accused because he was perplexed.
Within about 10 to 15 minutes, the witness named the accused and gave details of the occurrence.
The witness’s presence at the scene was not challenged.
issues.conclusion: The delay was reasonably explained by the witness’s shock and did not undermine his credibility or support an inference that he had not witnessed the attack.
issues.legal_principle: The credibility of an eyewitness must be assessed in context. A witness who is shocked or stunned by a ghastly occurrence may not be able to give names and details immediately; a brief, explained delay is not necessarily fatal to the account.

rule.if: criminal_case and eyewitness_saw_attack and eyewitness_delayed_naming and witness_explained_delay_by_shock and witness_later_named_assailants_and_gave_details

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned the prosecution of persons accused of a criminal attack.
predicates.eyewitness_saw_attack: A witness was present and saw the attack occur.
predicates.eyewitness_delayed_naming: The eyewitness did not name the assailants immediately after the attack.
predicates.witness_explained_delay_by_shock: The witness attributed the delay to being perplexed or shocked by the occurrence.
predicates.witness_later_named_assailants_and_gave_: After composing himself, the witness named the assailants and described the occurrence.

issues.definition: When a witness to a criminal attack briefly delays naming the assailants because of shock but later gives their names and details, the delay alone does not discredit the eyewitness.

issues.legal_issue: An extra-judicial confession must be assessed by its circumstances, timing, and the credibility of the witnesses, rather than presumed weak merely because it was made outside court.
material_facts: Two independent witnesses testified that an accused admitted to them that he had murdered the deceased.
The court found nothing in their evidence to suggest that they were untruthful.
Their evidence supported the eyewitness’s account.
issues.conclusion: The extra-judicial confession evidence was credible and, together with the eyewitness evidence, was sufficient to warrant conviction.
issues.legal_principle: A court must not begin with a presumption that an extra-judicial confession is weak evidence. Its weight depends on the circumstances in which it was made, when it was made, and the credibility of the witnesses who testify to it.

rule.if: criminal_case and extra_judicial_confession_to_witnesses and confession_witnesses_credible and confession_corrobates_eyewitness_account

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned the prosecution of persons accused of a criminal offence.
predicates.extra_judicial_confession_to_witnesses: An accused admitted involvement in the offence to witnesses outside court.
predicates.confession_witnesses_credible: The witnesses who recounted the confession were found credible.
predicates.confession_corrobates_eyewitness_account: The confession evidence supported an eyewitness’s account of the offence.

issues.definition: When credible witnesses recount an accused’s extra-judicial confession and it supports an eyewitness account, the confession can support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A weapon recovered at an accused’s instance and found to bear human blood is admissible recovery evidence that can corroborate other evidence of guilt.
material_facts: Weapons were recovered on the basis of statements made by the accused.
The recovered weapons bore blood which was found to be human blood.
The recovery evidence reinforced both the extra-judicial confession evidence and the eyewitness’s account.
issues.conclusion: The recoveries were admissible under the Evidence Act and corroborated the prosecution evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the recoveries made at the accused’s instance as admissible under the Evidence Act and as a circumstance supporting the truth of the prosecution case. The judgment does not identify a particular section or earlier case for this proposition.

rule.if: criminal_case and weapon_recovered_at_accused_instance and recovered_weapon_bore_human_blood and other_evidence_links_accused_to_offence

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned the prosecution of persons accused of a criminal offence.
predicates.weapon_recovered_at_accused_instance: A weapon was recovered on information or a statement provided by an accused.
predicates.recovered_weapon_bore_human_blood: Testing showed that the recovered weapon bore human blood.
predicates.other_evidence_links_accused_to_offence: Other evidence, such as an eyewitness account or confession evidence, connected the accused to the offence.

issues.definition: When a weapon is recovered at an accused’s instance, bears human blood, and other evidence connects the accused to the offence, the recovery is admissible and corroborative.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment acquitting an accused may be reversed on appeal when it rests on perverse or legally erroneous assessments of the evidence rather than a reasonable view of the case.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the eyewitness account because the witness did not immediately name the assailants and after treating extra-judicial confession evidence as inherently weak.
The appellate court considered the eyewitness evidence, credible confession evidence, and recoveries of weapons bearing human blood and reversed the acquittal.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s assessment unrealistic, legally erroneous, and based on wrong assumptions.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting the accused; the Supreme Court upheld the convictions and sentences.
issues.legal_principle: The court invoked the principle that an acquittal should not be disturbed where two views are reasonably possible. It held that this restraint does not bar appellate interference where the acquittal is perverse, legally erroneous, or based on wrong assumptions; it relied on no specifically named earlier case.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_unrealistic_or_wrong_: The acquittal rested on an unrealistic assessment of evidence or an incorrect assumption about its legal weight.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_supported_by_eyewit: The prosecution evidence included an eyewitness account supported by confession evidence, recovery evidence, or both.
predicates.acquittal_perverse_or_legally_erroneous: The acquittal was found to be perverse or legally erroneous rather than a reasonable view of the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, when the acquittal rests on unrealistic or legally mistaken assessments and the prosecution evidence supports guilt, an appellate court may reverse it if it is perverse or legally erroneous.
